title: The Cartographer's Confession
text:
Every map is an argument disguised as a description. The choice of projection, the decision about which settlements deserve a dot, the language in which a disputed river is labelled: none of these are neutral, and all of them are presented with the quiet authority of a technical document.

This is not a modern complaint. Medieval cartographers placed Jerusalem at the centre of the world and were entirely open about why. What changed is not the presence of bias but its visibility. Contemporary maps are produced by satellites and algorithms, and the machinery lends them an appearance of objectivity that their medieval ancestors never claimed.

The consequence is worth stating plainly. When a representation looks mechanical, we stop asking who made it and what they wanted. The most persuasive arguments in public life are rarely the loudest; they are the ones that have successfully arranged not to look like arguments at all.

title: On the Uses of Being Wrong in Public
text:
Scientific institutions are built on an unusual premise: that being publicly corrected is a form of professional success rather than humiliation. In practice, of course, the premise survives unevenly. Careers are made on being right, and retractions are counted as damage.

What makes the ideal worth defending is not politeness but efficiency. A field in which errors surface quickly converges faster than one in which they are buried under reputation management, however brilliant its individual members may be. The rate of progress depends less on the quality of hypotheses than on the speed at which bad ones are killed.

The difficulty is that this logic runs against nearly every incentive an individual faces. We are asked to behave as if our conclusions were disposable while being rewarded for defending them. That tension cannot be resolved by exhortation; it can only be managed by institutions that make correction cheap and stubbornness expensive.

title: The Attention Commons
text:
Economists have long understood the tragedy of the commons: a shared resource with no owner tends to be depleted, because each individual gains from taking more while the cost is distributed across everybody. Pastures, fisheries and aquifers all follow the pattern.

Human attention now behaves like such a commons, with one significant difference. The grazing is not done by the owners of the resource but by parties who have never met them, and who compete with increasing sophistication for something the owner cannot easily price. Every notification is a small enclosure of land that was, in principle, yours.

Proposed remedies tend to fall into two camps. The first asks individuals to build fences: digital hygiene, disciplined routines, devices left in another room. The second argues that no commons in history has ever been saved by the virtue of its users alone, and that the relevant question is regulatory rather than personal. The historical record, uncomfortably for the self-improvement industry, favours the second.
